summary: This nginx configuration sets up a secure web server for a Docusaurus documentation site. It redirects all unencrypted HTTP traffic to HTTPS, serves pre-rendered static files from a build directory, and includes smart routing logic that only falls back to index.html for dynamically generated tag and series pages—avoiding the common SPA pitfall of returning 200 OK for every URL.

explanations.8: The $host variable is the domain name the user requested, and $request_uri is the full path they asked for; this reconstructs the complete URL under HTTPS so users end up at the same place.
explanations.13: This server listens on port 443 (HTTPS) and enables http2, a faster version of the HTTP protocol that requires encryption.
explanations.25: The ssl_certificate points to the public cert file; in Docker, you mount your real certificates here at runtime so nginx can serve them without baking them into the image.
explanations.29: These settings lock nginx to only use modern, secure encryption standards; TLSv1.2 and TLSv1.3 are the safe versions, and older ones are disabled.
explanations.34: This adds a custom header to every response that identifies the server; it's cosmetic and harmless, just a signature.
explanations.38: The equals sign makes this match only the exact root path /, not /anything-else; so only visiting the bare domain triggers the redirect to /blog.
explanations.64: This regex matches paths like /series/my-series or /blog/tags/javascript, but only if there's one path segment after the slash (no nested subdirs); Docusaurus plugins generate these pages dynamically.
explanations.65: try_files attempts to serve $uri as a file, then $uri/ as a directory, and only if both fail does it serve /index.html so React Router can handle the page.
explanations.72: If the requested path isn't a real file or directory, serve a 404 error instead of pretending it exists; this tells search engines and link checkers the page is genuinely gone.
explanations.78: The internal directive hides 404.html from being directly requested by users; they see it only when nginx internally serves it for a missing page.
explanations.83: expires 1y tells the browser to cache these files for one year since they're immutable—their names change when content updates, so old cached versions won't cause stale data.
